title: Analogies for Learning
author: Blake Harvard
summary: Blake Harvard tackles a familiar classroom motivation problem: students know retrieval practice works better than rereading or highlighting, but keep choosing the easier, less effective methods anyway. His solution is to use analogies drawn from students' own hobbies -- he walks through a detailed musical-performance example -- to make the abstract case for retrieval concrete and personally relevant. The analogy compares cramming by rereading sheet music the night before a performance to rereading notes before a test, versus the effortful, repeated practice a musician actually needs to prepare properly. Harvard argues that framing retrieval practice this way helps students accept that getting things wrong during practice is a feature, not a failure, since it's far better to discover a gap during practice than during the real test or performance. He closes by inviting readers to share their own analogies and anecdotes for motivating better study habits.
points: Harvard's core insight is that retrieval practice has a motivation problem, not just a knowledge problem -- most students already sort of know it's better, but choose easier, less effective study methods anyway because they're more pleasant.

The musical-performance analogy works because it borrows a domain (sport, music, dance) where students already accept that repeated, effortful practice -- including plenty of mistakes -- is simply what preparation looks like.

His framing reverses the emotional valence of getting an answer wrong during practice: it becomes evidence of preparation working correctly, not evidence of failure, because it's far better to find gaps in practice than on the test.

Harvard explicitly generalizes the technique beyond music to any hobby a student is personally invested in -- sport, dance, acting, art -- making the analogy a flexible motivational tool rather than a single fixed script.
quotes: Over a century of research and practical usage by teachers in the classroom speak to the positive benefits of retrieval practice on retention of information.

But, it can sometimes be difficult to motivate students to invest in the more cognitively demanding efforts of retrieval practice instead of the ever-popular, yet less effective, methods of rereading and/or highlighting of notes.
You are going to practice playing the music many, many times over a period of several days or weeks. When you practice, you are going to get some of the notes correct.
Retrieval of content to prepare for the test is the equivalent of playing through the music to prepare for the performance.
You'd rather find out you don't know something during practice than find out on the test or during the performance…at that point, it's too late.
I've found that making the analogy to some hobby students really care about can help them to better understand the importance of proper studying and motivate students to put in the effort.
